comparison: Both evaluate age-related structural changes in bone (C1, C16-C18). OpenEval focuses specifically on microCT data showing BV/TV decreases and parietal thickness increases. Peer review groups these with broader age-related changes including osteoprogenitor depletion (C2, C31) and vascular/mechanical changes (C19-C30), praising the comprehensive characterization using scRNA-seq and quantitative assessments.

Both address osteoprogenitor depletion with age (C2, C31). OpenEval evaluates this claim separately with immunofluorescence data. Peer review groups it with other age-related changes (C1-C4, C16-C30) as part of fundamental findings supported by rigorous analyses.

Both evaluate age-related vascular changes (C19-C24). OpenEval focuses on decreased Emcn+ area, vessel number, and vascular calculations. Peer review groups these with broader age-related structural and cellular changes as fundamental findings.

Both address suture mesenchyme vascular stability (C25-C26). OpenEval evaluates this as a separate finding contrasting with periosteal decline. Peer review includes it within comprehensive age-related characterization.

Both evaluate morphological changes suggesting altered tissue mechanics (C27-C29). OpenEval focuses on nuclear aspect ratio, F-actin, and Lamin B1 data. Peer review groups these with other age-related changes as part of fundamental findings.

OpenEval evaluates functional decline markers in aged CD90+ cells (C3, C71-C81) with protein-level measurements. Peer review groups C3 with other age-related changes but does not separately address the detailed functional markers (C71-C81), which are covered in R5 and R12.

Both address mitochondrial dysfunction in aged osteoprogenitors. OpenEval includes specific markers (C71-C74: decreased ATPB, increased phospho-AMPK) as part of comprehensive functional decline. Peer review R5 identifies mitochondrial dysfunction (C71-C74) as a key mechanistic finding central to the therapeutic approach.

Both evaluate cellular aging markers (C75-C81). OpenEval includes loss of Ki67+, increased p16, reduced nuclear β-catenin, and decreased MMP2 as evidence of functional decline. Peer review accepts these as demonstrating 'intrinsic cellular deficits' as part of comprehensive cellular phenotyping.

Both evaluate age-dependent bone repair deficits (C4, C32-C35). OpenEval focuses on microCT data showing differential responses to Wnt3a-bandage across ages. Peer review emphasizes this demonstrates intrinsic cellular deficits and the need for combined interventions, highlighting the modest improvement in aged mice with Wnt3a alone.

Both address the disconnect between Wnt3a-induced cell expansion and functional repair in aged mice (C5-C6, C37-C41). OpenEval shows Wnt3a increases CD90+ cells and activates signaling but repair remains impaired. Peer review explicitly states 'Simply increasing the number of these cells does not restore their regenerative capacity,' confirming intrinsic deficits.

OpenEval evaluates improved bone quality with histological evidence (C36). Peer review groups this with other repair outcomes demonstrating the need for combined approaches to achieve functional restoration.

Both evaluate the synergistic effect of IF+Wnt3a-bandage restoring bone repair in aged mice (C7, C89-C91). OpenEval shows 67.10% repair comparable to young mice. Peer review celebrates this as the central 'remarkable finding' with all reviewers praising the combined approach that 'remarkably restores bone healing.'

OpenEval addresses the novelty of short-term post-injury IF intervention (C179-C183) including C182 about improved repair. Peer review R3 accepts C182 as part of the central finding about IF+Wnt3a restoring healing in aged animals.

Both evaluate IF-induced functional improvements in aged osteoprogenitors (C8, C118-C124). OpenEval shows increased ATPB, decreased phospho-AMPK, Ki67+ cells, nuclear β-catenin, and MMP2. Peer review confirms IF 'enhances osteoprogenitor function by targeting NAD+ pathways and gut microbiota, addressing mitochondrial dysfunction.'

Both evaluate IF-induced structural and cellular improvements (C92-C98). OpenEval shows increased BV/TV, Emcn+ area, CD90+ proportions, and reversed morphological aging markers. Peer review confirms IF 'improves osteoprogenitor function by rescuing aging-related mitochondrial dysfunction' with comprehensive molecular and cellular evidence.

Both evaluate mitochondrial dysfunction in aged osteoprogenitors (C11, C30, C53-C56). OpenEval presents converging evidence from TMRM staining, transcriptomics, and UCell scoring. Peer review explicitly identifies 'mitochondrial dysfunction in the age-related decline of stem cells' as a key finding and mechanistic foundation for the therapeutic approach.

Both evaluate NMN supplementation effects (C9, C125-C133). OpenEval shows NMN improves mitochondrial membrane potential, BV/TV, bone repair (54.32% with inactive bandage, 71.18% with Wnt3a), CD90+ cells, and vascularity. Peer review confirms benefits 'can be recapitulated by modulating NAD+ pathways,' validating NMN as a mechanistic proxy for IF.

Both evaluate NMN's protective effects on mitochondrial function and osteogenesis (C13, C139-C145). OpenEval shows NMN mitigates oligomycin-induced deficits in ATP, ROS, proliferation, preserves mitochondrial morphology, and enhances ALP/mineralization. Peer review accepts these as mechanistic validation supporting the NAD+ pathway role.

Both evaluate Akkermansia supplementation effects (C10, C146, C150-C162). OpenEval shows Akkermansia is elevated during IF, supplementation improves microbiome composition, BV/TV, bone repair (43.76% with inactive bandage, 64.84% with Wnt3a), CD90+ cells, and vascularity. Peer review confirms benefits 'can be achieved by modulating the gut microbiota,' accepting Akkermansia as another mechanistic pathway.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about Akkermansia and SCFAs (C147-C149, C152) as appropriately cited contextual knowledge. Peer review groups these with experimental Akkermansia findings, accepting the characterization as established literature supporting the gut microbiome mechanism.

Perfect agreement on cyclical nutrient deprivation effects (C12, C134-C138). Both evaluate in vitro data showing improved mitochondrial biogenesis, fusion, mitophagy gene expression, increased filament length and membrane potential. Reviewers accept this as mechanistic validation of in vivo IF effects with no questions raised.

OpenEval finds C14 (cyclical nutrient deprivation enhances osteogenesis) UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct osteogenesis assays, while C15 (NMN enhances osteogenesis) is SUPPORTED. Peer review R9 accepts both C13 and C15 as SUPPORTED, confirming 'Nicotinamide mononucleotide rejuvenate mitochondrial health, enhancing osteogenesis' without distinguishing the evidence levels for cyclical deprivation alone.

Both evaluate NMN's effects on mitochondrial health and osteogenesis (C13, C15 overlap). OpenEval provides detailed in vitro mechanistic data. Peer review accepts these findings as supporting the overall mechanism, noting 'robust methodologies across molecular, cellular, and tissue-level analyses.'

Both evaluate CD90+ cell characterization and SSC marker expression (C42-C46). OpenEval shows scRNAseq data with expression of Prrx1, Ctsk, Ddr2, and other progenitor markers. Peer review specifically praises 'the use of single-cell RNA sequencing to profile osteoprogenitor populations' as a major strength.

Both evaluate CD90+ subpopulation heterogeneity (C58-C63). OpenEval shows P1 cells express osteogenic markers while P2 cells express stemness markers. Peer review accepts the detailed characterization of distinct subpopulations as part of comprehensive scRNAseq analysis praised for profiling osteoprogenitor populations.

Both evaluate Igf1high/low population distributions and functional profiles (C64-C70). OpenEval shows age-dependent shifts and distinct gene expression patterns. Peer review accepts this heterogeneity characterization as part of the comprehensive scRNAseq profiling that enables identification of critical age-related deficits.

Both evaluate upregulated genes in young vs aged cells (C47-C49). OpenEval shows enrichment for cytosolic ribosome and collagen-containing ECM. Peer review accepts these transcriptomic findings as part of comprehensive characterization using 'advanced histological, transcriptomic, and functional assays.'

Both evaluate Wnt pathway component downregulation with age (C50-C52). OpenEval shows Wnt2 and Lrp6 downregulation. Peer review accepts these findings as supporting the rationale for Wnt3a-bandage intervention, which all reviewers endorse.

Both evaluate metabolic pathway specificity (C57). OpenEval shows no changes in glycolysis or lipid metabolism signatures, establishing specificity of mitochondrial defects. Peer review accepts this as part of transcriptomic characterization supporting the mitochondrial dysfunction focus.

Perfect agreement on IF protocol characterization (C82-C88). Both evaluate data showing IF is distinct from caloric restriction with no difference in total intake but lower fasting glucose and improved glucose tolerance. Reviewers accept the IF protocol as appropriately designed and implemented with no questions raised.

Both evaluate IF-induced transcriptomic changes in periosteum (C99-C105). OpenEval shows upregulated genes enriched for cytokine response. Peer review accepts these mechanistic findings as explaining how IF improves osteoprogenitor function, with Reviewer 3 noting the study 'enables the authors to identify critical age-related deficits.'

Both evaluate IF-induced transcriptomic changes in suture (C106-C112). OpenEval shows enrichment for cell cycle genes, Mki67 upregulation, and circadian transcription factors. Peer review accepts these molecular mechanisms including circadian rhythm findings without question as adding mechanistic depth.

Both evaluate IF-induced transcriptomic rejuvenation (C113-C117). OpenEval shows Aged+IF cells at 70.3% Igf1high, intermediate between young and aged, with partial reversal of aging signatures. Peer review accepts this as demonstrating how IF improves function through transcriptomic changes.

Perfect agreement on experimental model rationale (C163-C166). Both evaluate age group selection and female mouse model as appropriate. Peer review specifically praises 'the use of very old animals (up to 88 weeks, almost 2 years) modelling the human bone aging' as an important strength and clinically relevant model.

Perfect agreement on contextual background claims (C167-C178). Both evaluate these literature-based claims as appropriate framing. Peer review notes the study is 'a strong example of translational research' that builds on established knowledge, accepting the cited literature without question.

Both evaluate the novelty of IF intervention in aged animals (C179-C181, C183). OpenEval emphasizes distinction from long-term prevention studies. Peer review specifically notes 'here the authors provide evidence that in an already-aged animal, intermittent fasting can restore healing to levels seen in younger animals. This is an important finding,' accepting the novelty claims.

Both evaluate IF's impact on tissue mechanics (C184-C186). OpenEval shows transcriptomic and morphological evidence suggesting mechanical changes. Peer review accepts the overall novelty and mechanistic insights without specifically addressing the tissue mechanics inference.

Both evaluate circadian rhythm connections (C187-C193). OpenEval cites ChIP-SEQ and circadian literature linking transcription factors to Wnt signaling. Peer review accepts the mechanistic depth and novelty of diet-circadian interactions in bone repair as appropriately contextualized.

Perfect agreement on novelty claims regarding prior IF studies (C194-C198). Both evaluate the distinction between prevention and intervention paradigms. Peer review's comment about the 'remarkable finding' in aged animals implicitly accepts that the current study extends beyond previous work as appropriately framed.
